message.content:
Read-only Rust performance hunt on caliper. Goal from the owner: identify HOT SPOTS, MISSED OPPORTUNITIES and BAD PATTERNS that would yield more speed WITHOUT sacrificing results (output must stay byte-identical). This is not an architecture review: only findings that convert to measurable speed or memory wins.
Setup: repo /Users/gabe/Projects/caliper; in your worktree run `git fetch origin && git checkout --detach origin/perf/checker-shared-bases` (current head of the speed stack: checker default; whole-project extract 1.43 s gate-large / 1.07 s Chakra-only with the checker, 0.10 s with `--no-checker`; RDT 7.2 / 4.0 s). Do NOT edit or commit repo files, push, or open PRs. Report to ~/Projects/caliper-fixtures/perf-analysis/report.md (no /tmp). Use `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=$HOME/Projects/caliper-fixtures/perf-analysis/target`, Rust 1.99.1 first on PATH (/Users/gabe/.rustup/toolchains/1.99.1-aarch64-apple-darwin/bin; the mise shim forces 1.98.1), release builds, outside the sandbox where needed. No oracle runs, no corpus fetches. Fixtures: ~/Projects/caliper-fixtures/gate-large/src and ~/Projects/caliper-fixtures/checker-default/chakra-only/src; earlier scratch (profiles, ab.sh, measure.py, samply setup) in ~/Projects/caliper-fixtures/extract-speed/.
Method: profile, do not guess. (1) Checker path `extract --json --quiet --no-cache` on both fixtures: CPU profile (samply) of Caliper's own threads AND the checker threads; list the top self-time and inclusive-time frames, allocation counts and bytes by site (scratch allocator wrapper or dhat in a scratch copy, not the repo), peak RSS composition. (2) Structural path `--no-checker` (0.10 s: where is it spent, is process start / Node-free startup / file discovery / oxc parse / canonical JSON writing dominant?), `--format rdt`, and `--load-dependencies`. (3) Rerun path (0.25 s kept answer): what is in the 0.25 s vs the 0.10 s `--no-checker` floor (target: close to it). (4) Storybook/session path: cold first answer (171-189 ms, target 150 ms) and watch `ButtonProps` p95 (~172 ms, target 25 ms): time breakdown per phase using crates/semantic/examples/gate_harness.rs (first-answer and watch modes). (5) Static scan for bad patterns that the profile makes costly: per-item String/Vec/BTreeMap allocation in hot loops, clone of large structures, SipHash on hot maps (HashMap default hasher) where an Fx/ahash hasher is safe, repeated path normalization or UTF-8 validation, serde_json::Value round trips at the checker seam, Mutex/channel contention, small-granularity rayon, needless sorting, repeated parsing of the same file, regex compilation in loops, formatting via format! in hot paths, O(n^2) searches over Vec, large enum variants, double work between the structural pass and the checker merge. (6) Build and binary: whether compile flags/features (codegen-units, lto, target-cpu not applicable for distribution, `panic=unwind` required by guards) leave anything on the table; binary size drivers (CLI 34 MB). Skip anything already done or already measured as no gain: merge memo, per-snapshot prop cache, 2 checker programs with 4 converter threads, per-symbol type lookup once per snapshot, kept references, 8 files in flight, the on-disk kept answer, mimalloc in the CLI, fat LTO (no gain), batching (checker threads saturated), streaming output (peak is at the end of answering), Arc sharing of memo (clone is 1.7% of converter samples), simd-json (JSON parse is 9.7% of converter samples).
Output (report file and final message): a ranked list of findings, each with: title; evidence (file:line plus profile numbers, each marked MEASURED or ESTIMATED); expected gain in time or RSS and confidence; effort (S/M/L); how to prove output identity (full-content diff on both fixtures, determinism, construct lane); risk. Add a short 'checked and fine' list (hotspots that are already efficient, with the number) so we stop suspecting them. Be skeptical; label guesses as guesses. Final message: the top 10 findings, 2-3 lines each, plus the report path.

Only a SubagentHandback call reaches your caller as your result; plain text you write at the end is not delivered. Do not also send the report with SendMessage: your caller would get it twice.

#!/bin/zsh
# Usage: ab.sh <runs> <binary>... — interleaved whole-project extract (--json --quiet --no-cache) on gate-large and
# Chakra-only, wall seconds and peak RSS MiB from /usr/bin/time -l, one line per run.
runs=$1; shift
cd /Users/gabe/Projects/caliper-fixtures/extract-speed
for i in $(seq $runs); do
  for bin in "$@"; do
    for project in gate-large chakra-only; do
      case $project in
        gate-large) src=../gate-large/src ;;
        chakra-only) src=../checker-default/chakra-only/src ;;
      esac
      out=$(/usr/bin/time -l $bin extract --src $src --json --quiet --no-cache 2>&1 >/dev/null)
      real=$(echo "$out" | awk '/real/ {print $1}')
      rss=$(echo "$out" | awk '/maximum resident/ {printf "%d", $1/1048576}')
      cpu=$(echo "$out" | awk "/real/ {print \$3+\$5}")
      echo "$project $(basename $bin) ${real}s ${rss}MiB cpu=${cpu}s load=$(sysctl -n vm.loadavg | awk "{print \$2}")"
    done
  done
done

content.content:
# Performance

How fast Caliper is and what it costs is recorded in `docs/measurement.md`: a weekly run on five pinned corpora, and `just bench` for a change that touches the resolver. Both run the default, the checker (ADR 0026 S8); the figures below are the structural resolver's (`--no-checker`), measured before that and by hand, and the checker's cost is in `docs/gate-measurements.md` ("The checker is the default") and, once recorded, in the weekly. The criterion benches (`cargo bench -p caliper-docgen-core`) and `docs/benchmarks.md` cover single fixtures. This page keeps the measurements that explain where the time goes.

The per-pull-request scorecard that used to enforce these numbers is gone. It caught one real regression (Mantine 38% and Chakra 47% slower after a batch of 20 resolver pull requests merged on 2026-10-26, found by the weekly run), and its gates failed on runner noise and on bases that had moved. The figures below came from it and are history, not limits.

## Size model

Extraction time fits t ≈ 6.4 ms + 0.13 ms/kLOC + 3.8 ms/kprop (props summed over components). It is a sizing guide, reported by the old scorecard as "Model ms", never a gate: a fixed cost that varies by machine dominates small corpora, so per-corpus residuals vary too much to gate on. On the run below the model is within 2× of the measured extract time on every corpus (0.45× for mantine to 1.6× for chakra).

## Results, 2026-10-22

Apple Silicon laptop, macOS, load average 8 to 12, 10 runs per corpus, branch `ci/size-normalized-gates`.

| Corpus | kLOC | Components | Props | Unresolved | Wall ms | Extract ms | Peak RSS MB | Model ms | RDT ms | vs RDT |
| --- | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| mantine | 79.6 | 355 | 19,763 | 146 | 63.6 | 41.5 | 153 | 92 | 1,263 | 20× |
| chakra | 40.8 | 600 | 560 | 403 | 33.6 | 23.0 | 66 | 14 | 1,321 | 39× |
| shadcn | 489.6 | 2,140 | 1,615 | 1,526 | 80.1 | 64.0 | 104 | 76 | 1,906 | 24× |
| antd | 172.4 | 365 | 3,514 | 316 | 61.3 | 48.0 | 87 | 42 | 1,014 | 17× |
| spectrum | 256.6 | 1,482 | 7,031 | 1,901 | 80.9 | 60.0 | 116 | 66 | 1,787 | 22× |

Scaling: one copy of mantine 26 ms, two copies 46 ms (1.77×).

RDT's component and prop counts are not comparable with Caliper's here: without dependencies it reports every exported function and expands what it can of `@types/react`. Precision is in `docs/precision.md`; recall and agreement with RDT on installed repos are recorded weekly (`docs/measurement.md`).

## Dependency loading against RDT, 2026-10-23

Whether `--load-dependencies` can become the default (ADR 0010). The five repos with their dependencies installed, RDT run on the same component files through each repo's sources (`skipLibCheck`, dependencies resolvable), Caliper in RDT's format with `--html-attributes full`. The 20 fixture libraries can't answer this: they are single copied files with no installed packages.

| Corpus | RDT props Caliper reports, off → on | Unresolved warnings, off → on | Shared props whose type text changed: agree → disagree / disagree → agree | Wall ms, off → on | Peak RSS MiB, off → on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| mantine | 21.8% → 21.8% | 16 → 12 | 1 / 0 | 52 → 56 | 105 → 108 |
| chakra | 0.1% → 62.4% | 325 → 27 | 0 / 0 | 43 → 497 | 82 → 1,341 |
| shadcn | 0.2% → 4.5% | 829 → 265 | 6 / 2 | 67 → 104 | 104 → 176 |
| antd | 59.2% → 72.3% | 116 → 53 | 4 / 1 | 61 → 70 | 110 → 126 |
| spectrum | 97.1% → 97.1% | 174 → 166 | 0 / 0 | 116 → 121 | 191 → 215 |

- **Accuracy passes.** Coverage of RDT's props rises and unresolved names fall; of about 59,000 props both modes report, 11 stop matching RDT's text. All 11 are a named object or union type from a package that now prints expanded (`{ type: "file"; … }` for `FileUIPart`), which is how a project-declared object alias already prints (#104); RDT prints the name.
- **Fixed in #136: 497 ms and 1.3 GB became 255 ms and 0.3 GB.** Most of the cost was `keyof` walks resolving every member's type when only the names are read, and memo replays copying each recording's diagnostics into every component.
- **Chakra's peak memory with dependencies, by change** (`/usr/bin/time -l`, default threads): 367 MiB before the literal-type work, 494 MiB after member reads through csstype's `Fallback<T>` (#144), 388 MiB once an alias's arguments are resolved once and equal props are shared. Peak memory scales with threads (248 MiB on one thread, 388 on 18) because each thread holds the types it is building; measure memory before and after any change that evaluates more types, not only time.
- **Chakra's cost blocks the default.** Loaded dependencies let each of Chakra's 600 components reach its own ~705-prop style system: 398,000 props, 497 ms and 1.3 GB (RDT: 637,000 props, 27 s, 2.7 GB). `--collapse-inherited-props all` cuts that to 5,515 props but still 281 ms and 835 MiB, so most of the cost is not the listed props.

RDT (`withCustomConfig`, `shouldExtractLiteralValuesFromEnum`, `shouldRemoveUndefinedFromOptional`) took 1.6 to 27 s and 0.6 to 2.7 GB per repo. The harness that ran this is not in the repository; `scripts/weekly.py` records the same comparison.

## Storybook addon request path, 2026-10-24

Where the addon's time went, and what changed. Method: the `caliper-never` variant of the parity measurement (`docs/storybook-parity.md`), which answers every component, with the previous build and its binding before, interleaved with after, best of 3, Apple silicon. Peak RSS is the child process's.

| Corpus, story set                 | Metric           | Before     | After      |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------- | ---------- | ---------- |
| Spectrum, 129 real stories        | total            | 2.17 s     | 0.63 s     |
|                                   | median per story | 15 ms      | 4 ms       |
|                                   | first request    | 200 ms     | 150 ms     |
|                                   | peak RSS         | 354 MB     | 322 MB     |
| Spectrum, 90 sampled              | total            | 1.67 s     | 0.42 s     |
| shadcn, sampled                   | total / median   | 641 / 5 ms | 335 / 2 ms |
| antd, sampled                     | total / median   | 421 / 4 ms | 273 / 2 ms |
| Mantine, sampled                  | total / median   | 164 / 6 ms | 134 / 2 ms |
| Chakra with dependencies, sampled | total            | 1.16 s     | 0.80 s     |
|                                   | first request    | 527 ms     | 342 ms     |
|                                   | peak RSS         | 828 MB     | 681 MB     |

What the profile found:

- **The per-request file sweep was the cost.** `fresh()` listed every directory and stat'ed every source file from JavaScript on each story request (16–22 ms on Spectrum), and again for each subcomponent. The session now does one native check per story (`ensureFresh`), stat calls in parallel: 3–5 ms on Spectrum. `look at the files` is still the largest per-story cost on a large project.
- **Session start parsed every prop.** `initializeSession` returned all components' props as JSON for JavaScript to read two fields from: 25 MB and about 120 ms of `JSON.parse` for Chakra with dependencies. `initializeSessionIndex` returns the file, name and diagnostics only.
- **Allocation.** `mimalloc` in the binding cuts session start by 15–30% (Chakra with dependencies 441–561 ms → 312–391 ms) and Chakra's peak by 9%. On small projects the peak is 20–30 MB higher.
- **Left to the resolver.** On Chakra with dependencies the time is in resolution: the largest self-time entries are `StateReads::append` (dependency read tracking), `ParsedProp` map building (773 props per component) and memcpy. Sampled with `sample(1)`; not changed here.
- **Not a cost:** `keyOf` and `degradedBy` (microseconds, now indexed), `docgenInfo` (0.05–0.1 ms per component, 2–3 ms on Chakra's 358 KB documents), the JavaScript side of a story (about 4 ms of CPU, the rest is waiting on native work).

## Lazy sessions, 2026-10-24

`WatchSession::lazy` (ADR 0016) against `WatchSession::new(..).initialize()` on the corpora above, with `load_dependencies` and full HTML attributes (the richest answer). `cargo run --release -p caliper-docgen-core --example lazy_bench` runs one scenario per process; 50 components are chosen by a fixed seed. Apple Silicon laptop, parse cache and dependency index warm, best of 5 interleaved runs (spectrum: best of 3 to 5 before merging main, so a range).

| Corpus | Components | Batch start | Lazy start | 1 component | 10 | 50, one at a time | 50 at once | Batch peak | Lazy peak after 50 |
| --- | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| mantine | 344 | 68 ms | 40 ms | 52 ms | 67 ms | 81 ms | 68 ms | 108 MiB | 89 MiB |
| chakra | 609 | 352 ms | 45 ms | 172 ms | 249 ms | 566 ms | 310 ms | 532 MiB | 137 MiB |
| shadcn | 1,892 | 111 ms | 67 ms | 67 ms | 128 ms | 353 ms | 96 ms | 162 MiB | 134 MiB |
| antd | 248 | 71 ms | 60 ms | 66 ms | 114 ms | 213 ms | 141 ms | 119 MiB | 119 MiB |
| spectrum | 1,356 | 102 to 145 ms | 66 to 110 ms | 66 to 110 ms | 179 to 230 ms | 375 to 465 ms | not run | 135 to 178 MiB | 122 to 144 MiB |

Times are time from process start to the last answer (start plus requests); peak is the process's peak RSS (`/usr/bin/time -l`). Without dependencies and with curated attributes, lazy start is 28 to 85 ms against 39 to 107 ms for batch, peak memory is 50 to 114 MiB against 69 to 146 MiB, and 50 components cost 3 to 25 ms.

Every answer the example returned matched the batch run's for the same key (a hash of the full entries and diagnostics), serially and at once. `crates/core/tests/lazy_parity.rs` checks every component of the fixtures and of the five corpora, both settings, at once and one at a time in forward and reverse order.

The earlier lazy-session measurements did not cover Spectrum with both options on after merging main or the NAPI binding (the example calls the Rust API the binding wraps). The whole-project runs below cover more than 50 components.

## Chained lazy dependency layers, 2026-10-25

On the five installed parity corpora, `lazy_bench` with dependency loading and full HTML attributes, best of three runs per scenario. `random50` asks 50 seeded components one at a time; `all` asks every listed component in key order. Peak RSS is per process. The comparison uses the same build with the whole-demand threshold at three or 48 growths; this change sets the threshold to three (design in `docs/architecture/pipeline-orchestration.md`, "Demand-driven dependencies").

| Corpus   | 50 requests: 3 → 48 growths | Peak MB: 3 → 48 | All requests: 3 → 48 | Peak MB: 3 → 48 |
| -------- | --------------------------: | --------------: | -------------------: | --------------: |
| Mantine  |                  30 → 27 ms |         68 → 67 |         163 → 170 ms |         88 → 84 |
| Chakra   |                234 → 271 ms |       107 → 105 |     2,117 → 2,384 ms |       317 → 317 |
| shadcn   |                  52 → 72 ms |        144 → 94 |         213 → 272 ms |       159 → 159 |
| antd     |                  18 → 46 ms |         71 → 73 |          56 → 126 ms |         81 → 84 |
| Spectrum |                  20 → 47 ms |        102 → 90 |         162 → 222 ms |       134 → 134 |

All ten output digests match across thresholds and the pre-chain build. The three-growth chain is also faster than the pre-chain three-growth build on 50 requests for all five corpora: 42 → 30 ms on Mantine, 313 → 234 on Chakra, 61 → 52 on shadcn, 23 → 18 on antd, and 27 → 20 on Spectrum. A file first parsed as a re-export stub must be indexed when later claimed; without that step, 28 shadcn components lost props in the whole-project run. The regression test and forward-order corpus parity check cover it.

## Default changes

Two defaults flipped after measurement. Both tables are history, not limits.

### Dependency loading on, 2026-10-25

`PipelineOptions::load_dependencies` defaults to `true` (the CLI, the config file, the Vite plugin, the NAPI binding and the addon; the addon already did). `--no-load-dependencies` turns it off, `--load-dependencies` still means the default, and a project with no packages installed loads nothing either way. It was off while Chakra took 497 ms and 1.3 GB with it on, against 43 ms and 82 MiB without; memo replay, `keyof` name walks, interned keys and a parallel lib parse (#136, #175, #177, #178, #182) took that to about 220 ms and 330 MiB. Five parity corpora, `extract --json`, best of 7, interleaved, on a laptop shared with other jobs (about ±10 ms), off → on:

| Corpus   |  Wall ms | Peak RSS MiB |           Props | Unresolved warnings |
| -------- | -------: | -----------: | --------------: | ------------------: |
| mantine  |  50 → 60 |    112 → 128 | 19,834 → 19,834 |             14 → 10 |
| chakra   | 50 → 220 |    101 → 330 |   592 → 479,235 |             315 → 0 |
| shadcn   |  50 → 90 |    101 → 225 |   1,543 → 8,131 |           816 → 190 |
| antd     |  40 → 50 |     95 → 114 |   3,349 → 3,856 |              76 → 8 |
| spectrum |  70 → 90 |    136 → 161 | 32,585 → 32,587 |              13 → 5 |

Output is exact: the new default is byte-identical to the previous build's `--load-dependencies` output, and `--no-load-dependencies` to the previous default. Share of react-docgen-typescript's props reported, off → on (the 0.4.0 baseline, since removed): Chakra 0.1% → 98.6%, shadcn 6.4% → 39.5%, antd 71.8% → 80.3%, Mantine and Spectrum 99.7% both. The cost lands on a few projects: Chakra is 4.4× slower and holds 3.3× the memory, shadcn takes 40 ms and 124 MiB more, the others 10 to 20 ms and 16 to 25 MiB. A CI job that needs the old speed passes `--no-load-dependencies`.

### Every HTML attribute listed, 2026-10-26

`PipelineOptions::html_attributes` defaults to `full` (the reasons are in `docs/rdt-coverage.md`, HtmlAttributeMode). Five parity corpora with dependencies loaded, canonical JSON, no cache, median of 11 (wall) and 21 (CPU, peak RSS), old default (`curated` at 338d1ddc) → new default:

| Corpus   |   Wall ms |       CPU s | Peak RSS MiB |     JSON MB |
| -------- | --------: | ----------: | -----------: | ----------: |
| antd     |   56 → 62 | 0.33 → 0.37 |    130 → 151 |   3.6 → 6.3 |
| chakra   | 424 → 470 | 3.13 → 3.72 |    514 → 577 | 11.1 → 16.7 |
| mantine  | 149 → 164 | 1.05 → 1.21 |    175 → 229 |  8.4 → 14.2 |
| spectrum |   90 → 98 | 0.68 → 0.73 |    171 → 191 |  8.3 → 11.7 |
| shadcn   | 144 → 188 | 1.28 → 1.72 |    220 → 301 |  5.9 → 12.2 |

The default is slower and larger than the old one at that commit: wall time +9 to +31%, peak RSS +12 to +37%, canonical JSON +42 to +105%. Most of the wall time was a lookup bug, fixed in #241 (indexing component lookups by name): shadcn `full` went from 153 to 127 ms, against 124 ms for the old default, with identical output. On the Storybook request path the first story was no slower with `full` than with `none`. Storybook parity (props Storybook lists that the addon lacks, antd / shadcn / Spectrum): 37 / 0 / 1 → 34 / 0 / 1. `ref` on `forwardRef` components written as `React.forwardRef(Inner)` is listed since #244; `PurePanel`'s 33 props, Drawer's own, remain because the declared type does not extend them.

| Corpus | RDT props Caliper reports, off → on | Unresolved warnings, off → on | Shared props whose type text changed: agree → disagree / disagree → agree | Wall ms, off → on | Peak RSS MiB, off → on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| mantine | 21.8% → 21.8% | 16 → 12 | 1 / 0 | 52 → 56 | 105 → 108 |
| chakra | 0.1% → 62.4% | 325 → 27 | 0 / 0 | 43 → 497 | 82 → 1,341 |
| shadcn | 0.2% → 4.5% | 829 → 265 | 6 / 2 | 67 → 104 | 104 → 176 |
| antd | 59.2% → 72.3% | 116 → 53 | 4 / 1 | 61 → 70 | 110 → 126 |
| spectrum | 97.1% → 97.1% | 174 → 166 | 0 / 0 | 116 → 121 | 191 → 215 |

- **Accuracy passes.** Coverage of RDT's props rises and unresolved names fall; of about 59,000 props both modes report, 11 stop matching RDT's text. All 11 are a named object or union type from a package that now prints expanded (`{ type: "file"; … }` for `FileUIPart`), which is how a project-declared object alias already prints (#104); RDT prints the name.
- **Fixed in #136: 497 ms and 1.3 GB became 255 ms and 0.3 GB.** Most of the cost was `keyof` walks resolving every member's type when only the names are read, and memo replays copying each recording's diagnostics into every component.
- **Chakra's peak memory with dependencies, by change** (`/usr/bin/time -l`, default threads): 367 MiB before the literal-type work, 494 MiB after member reads through csstype's `Fallback<T>` (#144), 388 MiB once an alias's arguments are resolved once and equal props are shared. Peak memory scales with threads (248 MiB on one thread, 388 on 18) because each thread holds the types it is building; measure memory before and after any change that evaluates more types, not only time.
- **Chakra's cost blocks the default.** Loaded dependencies let each of Chakra's 600 components reach its own ~705-prop style system: 398,000 props, 497 ms and 1.3 GB (RDT: 637,000 props, 27 s, 2.7 GB). `--collapse-inherited-props all` cuts that to 5,515 props but still 281 ms and 835 MiB, so most of the cost is not the listed props.

RDT (`withCustomConfig`, `shouldExtractLiteralValuesFromEnum`, `shouldRemoveUndefinedFromOptional`) took 1.6 to 27 s and 0.6 to 2.7 GB per repo. The harness that ran this is not in the repository; `scripts/weekly.py` records the same comparison.

## Storybook addon request path, 2026-10-24

Where the addon's time went, and what changed. Method: the `caliper-never` variant of the parity measurement (`docs/storybook-parity.md`), which answers every component, with the previous build and its binding before, interleaved with after, best of 3, Apple silicon. Peak RSS is the child process's.

| Corpus, story set                 | Metric           | Before     | After      |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------- | ---------- | ---------- |
| Spectrum, 129 real stories        | total            | 2.17 s     | 0.63 s     |
|                                   | median per story | 15 ms      | 4 ms       |
|                                   | first request    | 200 ms     | 150 ms     |
|                                   | peak RSS         | 354 MB     | 322 MB     |
| Spectrum, 90 sampled              | total            | 1.67 s     | 0.42 s     |
| shadcn, sampled                   | total / median   | 641 / 5 ms | 335 / 2 ms |
| antd, sampled                     | total / median   | 421 / 4 ms | 273 / 2 ms |
| Mantine, sampled                  | total / median   | 164 / 6 ms | 134 / 2 ms |
| Chakra with dependencies, sampled | total            | 1.16 s     | 0.80 s     |
|                                   | first request    | 527 ms     | 342 ms     |
|                                   | peak RSS         | 828 MB     | 681 MB     |

What the profile found:

- **The per-request file sweep was the cost.** `fresh()` listed every directory and stat'ed every source file from JavaScript on each story request (16–22 ms on Spectrum), and again for each subcomponent. The session now does one native check per story (`ensureFresh`), stat calls in parallel: 3–5 ms on Spectrum. `look at the files` is still the largest per-story cost on a large project.
- **Session start parsed every prop.** `initializeSession` returned all components' props as JSON for JavaScript to read two fields from: 25 MB and about 120 ms of `JSON.parse` for Chakra with dependencies. `initializeSessionIndex` returns the file, name and diagnostics only.
- **Allocation.** `mimalloc` in the binding cuts session start by 15–30% (Chakra with dependencies 441–561 ms → 312–391 ms) and Chakra's peak by 9%. On small projects the peak is 20–30 MB higher.
- **Left to the resolver.** On Chakra with dependencies the time is in resolution: the largest self-time entries are `StateReads::append` (dependency read tracking), `ParsedProp` map building (773 props per component) and memcpy. Sampled with `sample(1)`; not changed here.
- **Not a cost:** `keyOf` and `degradedBy` (microseconds, now indexed), `docgenInfo` (0.05–0.1 ms per component, 2–3 ms on Chakra's 358 KB documents), the JavaScript side of a story (about 4 ms of CPU, the rest is waiting on native work).

## Lazy sessions, 2026-10-24

`WatchSession::lazy` (ADR 0016) against `WatchSession::new(..).initialize()` on the corpora above, with `load_dependencies` and full HTML attributes (the richest answer). `cargo run --release -p caliper-docgen-core --example lazy_bench` runs one scenario per process; 50 components are chosen by a fixed seed. Apple Silicon laptop, parse cache and dependency index warm, best of 5 interleaved runs (spectrum: best of 3 to 5 before merging main, so a range).

| Corpus | Components | Batch start | Lazy start | 1 component | 10 | 50, one at a time | 50 at once | Batch peak | Lazy peak after 50 |
| --- | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| mantine | 344 | 68 ms | 40 ms | 52 ms | 67 ms | 81 ms | 68 ms | 108 MiB | 89 MiB |
| chakra | 609 | 352 ms | 45 ms | 172 ms | 249 ms | 566 ms | 310 ms | 532 MiB | 137 MiB |
| shadcn | 1,892 | 111 ms | 67 ms | 67 ms | 128 ms | 353 ms | 96 ms | 162 MiB | 134 MiB |
| antd | 248 | 71 ms | 60 ms | 66 ms | 114 ms | 213 ms | 141 ms | 119 MiB | 119 MiB |
| spectrum | 1,356 | 102 to 145 ms | 66 to 110 ms | 66 to 110 ms | 179 to 230 ms | 375 to 465 ms | not run | 135 to 178 MiB | 122 to 144 MiB |

Times are time from process start to the last answer (start plus requests); peak is the process's peak RSS (`/usr/bin/time -l`). Without dependencies and with curated attributes, lazy start is 28 to 85 ms against 39 to 107 ms for batch, peak memory is 50 to 114 MiB against 69 to 146 MiB, and 50 components cost 3 to 25 ms.

Every answer the example returned matched the batch run's for the same key (a hash of the full entries and diagnostics), serially and at once. `crates/core/tests/lazy_parity.rs` checks every component of the fixtures and of the five corpora, both settings, at once and one at a time in forward and reverse order.

The earlier lazy-session measurements did not cover Spectrum with both options on after merging main or the NAPI binding (the example calls the Rust API the binding wraps). The whole-project runs below cover more than 50 components.

## Chained lazy dependency layers, 2026-10-25

On the five installed parity corpora, `lazy_bench` with dependency loading and full HTML attributes, best of three runs per scenario. `random50` asks 50 seeded components one at a time; `all` asks every listed component in key order. Peak RSS is per process. The comparison uses the same build with the whole-demand threshold at three or 48 growths; this change sets the threshold to three (design in `docs/architecture/pipeline-orchestration.md`, "Demand-driven dependencies").

| Corpus   | 50 requests: 3 → 48 growths | Peak MB: 3 → 48 | All requests: 3 → 48 | Peak MB: 3 → 48 |
| -------- | --------------------------: | --------------: | -------------------: | --------------: |
| Mantine  |                  30 → 27 ms |         68 → 67 |         163 → 170 ms |         88 → 84 |
| Chakra   |                234 → 271 ms |       107 → 105 |     2,117 → 2,384 ms |       317 → 317 |
| shadcn   |                  52 → 72 ms |        144 → 94 |         213 → 272 ms |       159 → 159 |
| antd     |                  18 → 46 ms |         71 → 73 |          56 → 126 ms |         81 → 84 |
| Spectrum |                  20 → 47 ms |        102 → 90 |         162 → 222 ms |       134 → 134 |

All ten output digests match across thresholds and the pre-chain build. The three-growth chain is also faster than the pre-chain three-growth build on 50 requests for all five corpora: 42 → 30 ms on Mantine, 313 → 234 on Chakra, 61 → 52 on shadcn, 23 → 18 on antd, and 27 → 20 on Spectrum. A file first parsed as a re-export stub must be indexed when later claimed; without that step, 28 shadcn components lost props in the whole-project run. The regression test and forward-order corpus parity check cover it.

## Default changes

Two defaults flipped after measurement. Both tables are history, not limits.

### Dependency loading on, 2026-10-25

`PipelineOptions::load_dependencies` defaults to `true` (the CLI, the config file, the Vite plugin, the NAPI binding and the addon; the addon already did). `--no-load-dependencies` turns it off, `--load-dependencies` still means the default, and a project with no packages installed loads nothing either way. It was off while Chakra took 497 ms and 1.3 GB with it on, against 43 ms and 82 MiB without; memo replay, `keyof` name walks, interned keys and a parallel lib parse (#136, #175, #177, #178, #182) took that to about 220 ms and 330 MiB. Five parity corpora, `extract --json`, best of 7, interleaved, on a laptop shared with other jobs (about ±10 ms), off → on:

| Corpus   |  Wall ms | Peak RSS MiB |           Props | Unresolved warnings |
| -------- | -------: | -----------: | --------------: | ------------------: |
| mantine  |  50 → 60 |    112 → 128 | 19,834 → 19,834 |             14 → 10 |
| chakra   | 50 → 220 |    101 → 330 |   592 → 479,235 |             315 → 0 |
| shadcn   |  50 → 90 |    101 → 225 |   1,543 → 8,131 |           816 → 190 |
| antd     |  40 → 50 |     95 → 114 |   3,349 → 3,856 |              76 → 8 |
| spectrum |  70 → 90 |    136 → 161 | 32,585 → 32,587 |              13 → 5 |

Output is exact: the new default is byte-identical to the previous build's `--load-dependencies` output, and `--no-load-dependencies` to the previous default. Share of react-docgen-typescript's props reported, off → on (the 0.4.0 baseline, since removed): Chakra 0.1% → 98.6%, shadcn 6.4% → 39.5%, antd 71.8% → 80.3%, Mantine and Spectrum 99.7% both. The cost lands on a few projects: Chakra is 4.4× slower and holds 3.3× the memory, shadcn takes 40 ms and 124 MiB more, the others 10 to 20 ms and 16 to 25 MiB. A CI job that needs the old speed passes `--no-load-dependencies`.

### Every HTML attribute listed, 2026-10-26

`PipelineOptions::html_attributes` defaults to `full` (the reasons are in `docs/rdt-coverage.md`, HtmlAttributeMode). Five parity corpora with dependencies loaded, canonical JSON, no cache, median of 11 (wall) and 21 (CPU, peak RSS), old default (`curated` at 338d1ddc) → new default:

| Corpus   |   Wall ms |       CPU s | Peak RSS MiB |     JSON MB |
| -------- | --------: | ----------: | -----------: | ----------: |
| antd     |   56 → 62 | 0.33 → 0.37 |    130 → 151 |   3.6 → 6.3 |
| chakra   | 424 → 470 | 3.13 → 3.72 |    514 → 577 | 11.1 → 16.7 |
| mantine  | 149 → 164 | 1.05 → 1.21 |    175 → 229 |  8.4 → 14.2 |
| spectrum |   90 → 98 | 0.68 → 0.73 |    171 → 191 |  8.3 → 11.7 |
| shadcn   | 144 → 188 | 1.28 → 1.72 |    220 → 301 |  5.9 → 12.2 |

The default is slower and larger than the old one at that commit: wall time +9 to +31%, peak RSS +12 to +37%, canonical JSON +42 to +105%. Most of the wall time was a lookup bug, fixed in #241 (indexing component lookups by name): shadcn `full` went from 153 to 127 ms, against 124 ms for the old default, with identical output. On the Storybook request path the first story was no slower with `full` than with `none`. Storybook parity (props Storybook lists that the addon lacks, antd / shadcn / Spectrum): 37 / 0 / 1 → 34 / 0 / 1. `ref` on `forwardRef` components written as `React.forwardRef(Inner)` is listed since #244; `PurePanel`'s 33 props, Drawer's own, remain because the declared type does not extend them.

1:# Gate measurements
2:
3:**Last measured:** 2026-11-09 on `feat/gate-harness` at `f3784be5`, tsrs `0.23.0-ts7.1.0-beta` (the pin), macOS 27.3 on an Apple M5 Max (18 cores, 64 GiB). Two of the gates in [ADR 0026](adr/0026-the-checker-is-the-type-authority.md#gates-before-the-default-flips) need a measurement rather than a test: determinism on a large program and memory past 600 edits; S4 adds a third, the first answer on Chakra (measured on `feat/checker-wins`, see its section), and S6 a fourth, edit-and-query on the snapshot the checker keeps (measured on `feat/checker-watch`, see its section). This records how each was made measurable and what it read.
4:
5:Rerun them with `just gate-measure` (about 20 minutes), which also runs S6's watch gate. It builds the large project outside the repository (`GATE_FIXTURES`, default `~/Projects/caliper-fixtures/gate-large`, by `scripts/gate_fixtures.mjs`), builds `crates/semantic/examples/gate_harness.rs`, and prints one JSON line per gate. A gate that fails its own check exits 1; the recipe runs every gate and then fails if any did.
6:
7:## The program
8:
9:- `scripts/gate_fixtures.mjs` installs `@chakra-ui/react` 3.37.0 and `@mui/material` 9.5.0 (the root `package.json`'s pins) with `pnpm`, and writes one wrapper per exported component, `export function ChakraButton(props: ComponentProps<typeof Button>)`: 1,616 components (1,466 Chakra, 150 MUI). The Chakra and MUI sources themselves were not fetched, so this is not the Chakra corpus of `docs/measurement.md`: it is what an app that wraps both libraries asks the checker.
10:- Each request to the checker builds a program that loads one library's declarations whole, which is what makes it a large program.
11:- The harness uses the session a Storybook addon runs: a lazy `WatchSession` with `load_dependencies` on, nothing collapsed, and a warm `OnDemand` that waits up to 120 s, over the pinned tsrs binary the oracle's `tsrs-bin.ts` resolves.
12:
13:## Memory past 600 edits
14:
15:- **How.** `OnDemand` now counts its planned process replacements by cause (`recycles()`: `worn` after 64 programs, `bloated` after `max_rss_mib`) and reports the process that answered last (`process_id()`); each replacement is logged at debug level. The harness rewrites one component's file (`ButtonProps & { edit{n}: string }`, which makes the checker load Chakra), calls `update_file`, asks for the component, and reads the process's PID and resident memory from `ps` after every answer, 650 times. It then asks a fresh session over the final files and compares the two answers whole.
16:- **Result at the shipped bound (768 MiB):** 650 of 650 answers came from the checker and carried that edit's prop (0 stale). The checker ran as 11 processes, 10 replacements, all `worn` and none `bloated`. Peak resident memory was 446 MiB (452 MiB in an earlier run of the same command). The last answer equals the fresh session's.
17:- **What that shows, and what it does not.** The 64-program limit does the work on this program: a process reached 446 MiB at most, so the 768 MiB bound never fired. The gate asks for the bound to be exercised, so the harness takes `--max-rss-mib`. With 300: 49 `bloated` replacements, 50 processes, no `worn`, peak 331 MiB (a request that grows past the bound finishes first, and the check runs on every fourth request), and the last answer equals the fresh session's again.
18:- **Verdict: PASS** for what was measured (no leak past 650 edits, replacements keep the answers right, the memory bound works when crossed). Not measured: a program whose single process passes 768 MiB on its own, or a real watch session with the Storybook addon and Node in the loop.
19:
20:## Determinism across checker counts
21:
22:- **Not applicable as worded.** tsrs has no checker-count option on the path caliper uses. `tsrs --api --help` lists `-async`, `-callbacks`, `-cwd`, `-pipe`, `-runExternalCode`, `-timing` and `-useCaseSensitiveFileNames`, and `--api --checkers 2` is refused with `flag provided but not defined: -checkers`. The compile mode (`tsrs --checkers 2 -p .`) takes the flag, as `typescript@7.1.0-beta`'s `tsc --help --all` documents, but caliper never runs it: `supervisor.rs` starts `--api --async --cwd` and passes nothing else, and the only thread-count variable among the binary's strings is rayon's `RAYON_NUM_THREADS`.
23:- **Nearest measurable form.** The output must not depend on how the checker's parallelism is set, on the order components are asked in, or on which process answers. The harness asks a fresh tsrs process for 150 components (every tenth of the 1,616, sorted by key) with `RAYON_NUM_THREADS` set to 1, 2 and 4, three runs each, the middle run asking in reverse order, and byte-compares all nine outputs (each component's JSON entry and diagnostics, sorted by key). The variable changes the process: its thread count read 4, 5 and 7 at 1, 2 and 4. It does not change a checker count, which nothing here sets.
24:- **Result:** all nine outputs are identical, 341,396,960 bytes each. 148 of the 150 components were answered by the checker in every run; `MuiPopoverRoot` and `MuiSliderMark` kept their structural answer in every run (why the checker declined them was not investigated). So the checker's answers are identical across thread counts, runs, process restarts and query order.
25:- **Verdict: NOT MEASURABLE as worded; PASS in the nearest form.** The ADR's wording should read "output is deterministic across repeated runs, thread counts, restarts and query order on a large program" until tsrs exposes a count on `--api`. The compile-mode flag was not tried against a program, since its output is not what caliper reads.
26:
27:## First answer (S4)
28:
29:- **The gate.** S4: "Chakra first answer at most 150 ms through the Rust client", the addon's default `semanticWaitMs`, which decides whether a first story shows the checker's props or the structural ones.
30:- **How.** `gate_harness first-answer` (the third gate `just gate-measure` runs) opens, `--runs` times (default 5), a fresh lazy session configured as the addon configures it (dependencies loaded, nothing collapsed, the default `htmlAttributes`), starts the checker in the background as the addon does at creation, waits until that process is up and initialized, then times one `component("ChakraButton")`: the structural pass and the checker's program and conversion for that one component, through the same `OnDemand` the addon uses. It passes when every answer is the checker's and the median is at most `--budget-ms` (150).
31:- **Result (2026-11-09, `feat/checker-wins`, tsrs `0.23.0-ts7.1.0-beta`, 9 runs, a shared machine at load 13):** every answer was the checker's; median **562 ms** (557 to 575), of which the structural answer is 5 ms and the process start, already done before the request, 5 ms. **FAIL.**
32:- **Where the time goes.** One answer is about 4,400 requests to tsrs, one at a time: the props of `ButtonProps` are mostly Chakra's style props, each a distinct instantiated union (1,800 `getTypesOfType`, 1,250 `getTypeArguments`, 600 `typeToString`, 560 `batchRequests`, and 43 ms for the snapshot). A request takes about 70 µs, round trip included. Three changes were tried and not kept: converting 16 props at once (360 to 390 ms, but it changes which type handle first asks about a symbol, so the replay fixtures no longer match and would need recording again), batching the requests a level of the walk will make (no faster, so the cost is in the answering, not the round trips) and one documentation batch per component (5%). What would meet 150 ms is fewer requests per component, for example expanding a dependency's instantiated aliases on demand; that is converter work beyond S4.
33:- **Verdict: FAIL**, so ADR 0022's premise stands with tsrs: a story shows the structural props first and the checker's from the next request on.
34:
35:### Fewer and cheaper requests (2026-11-10, `perf/checker-first-answer`)
36:
37:- **Profile.** Every request of one answer logged with its time and answer: 5,271 requests (1,829 `getTypesOfType`, 1,254 `getTypeArguments`, 852 `getDocumentationComment`, 593 `typeToString`, 562 batches of an object's members). 679 of them repeated a request already answered: a type the memo converts again at another depth asks for its members or arguments again. The answers weigh 39 MB, and 31.6 MB of that is the property lists of 562 mapped types: each style prop is `ConditionalValue<V>`, whose condition map has 130 properties and is cut as too wide, which takes the list to count. The client parsed every answer three times: into a `Value`, into a `Value` again, then into its type.
38:- **What changed.** The client keeps an answer's `result` as text and the backend parses it once, into the type it expects (`Client::request_raw`). A type's members and type arguments are kept by type handle for the snapshot, as the checker's text, so a type converted again asks for neither again. One answer is now 4,593 requests. Output is byte-identical: the whole-program checker run on `gate-large` (938 components) gave the same bytes on main and the branch in 10 runs; the construct suite and checker lane pass; the replay fixtures were recorded again against the pinned tsrs, since the request set shrank.
39:- **Result:** median **402 ms** (395 to 434) against main's 535 ms (522 to 576), 9 interleaved runs each, every answer the checker's. **FAIL.** The whole-program checker run takes 13.1 s against 15.3 s (5 interleaved runs), the addon's configuration without the checker is unchanged, and peak memory did not grow: caliper 441 MiB against 434, tsrs 563 MiB against 576 (medians of 5 interleaved runs, sampled per process).
40:- **The other gates, re-run.** `just gate-measure` on the branch: memory PASS (650 of 650 answers the checker's, none stale, 11 processes, 10 `worn` replacements, last answer equal to a fresh session's, peak 478 MiB, then 444 in a second run, against main's 449 and 475 on the same day), determinism PASS (nine outputs of 341,419,093 bytes, all identical), first answer 400 ms over 5 runs, FAIL.

## Watch on `snapshot.update` (S6)

- **The gate.** "An unnotified edit fails a test loudly; Chakra edit-and-query p95 at most 25 ms; 300 Chakra edits stay under the threshold." What the slice changed is in [watch](type-checker-integration.md#watch-adr-0026-slice-s6): the warm checker keeps its snapshot and brings it up to date with `updateSnapshot`, and checks the files its program read against their stamps before each answer.
- **The protocol, probed first** (tsrs `0.23.0-ts7.1.0-beta` and the Go `7.1.0-beta`, `~/Projects/caliper-fixtures/s6/probe*.mjs`, a component of `ButtonProps & Extra & { editN }` whose program reads 1,855 files). `updateSnapshot` exists on both. A synthetic program sees nothing without `ensurePrograms: true`: notified or not, a `uri` or a path, `invalidateAll` and a `fileSystem` layer all answered the old text. With it, a notified file is read again and the response lists it under `changedFiles`; an unnotified one stays stale, and so does an unnotified file beside a notified one. A file created where an import failed resolves once announced as `created` or `changed`, and `deleted` removes one. On the Chakra program an update took 16.7 ms median and 26.7 ms p95 over 40 edits (Node client), against 36 to 38 ms for `createSnapshot`.
- **Loud failure.** `crates/semantic/tests/watch.rs` edits a file the component imports without telling the checker: the answer carries one `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` warning naming that file and has the new prop (read from a fresh snapshot). With the comparison disabled the same test fails (no warning, the old prop). It runs on tsrs in the checker lane and on the Go checker in Test / Rust; `crates/core/tests/semantic_hook.rs` holds that `update_file`, `ensure_fresh` and a rebuild each tell the checker.
- **How it was measured.** `gate_harness watch` (the fourth gate of `just gate-measure`): the memory gate's edit loop, `ButtonProps & { edit{n}: string }` rewritten, `update_file`, then the component, timed together, 300 times, with the checker's resident memory and CPU time read after each answer; then the checker's answer alone on its unchanged snapshot, and the edited component and every hundredth other one byte-compared with a fresh session asked in reverse order. `--props own` edits a component with one prop of its own in the same program, so the checker still loads Chakra whole but there is almost nothing to convert. The base is `feat/instantiation-probe` with the same harness (a `createSnapshot` per request).
- **Result, `ButtonProps` (2026-11-10, release builds, a shared machine at load 10 to 29).** 300 of 300 answers the checker's, none stale, none warned, 296 from updated snapshots and 5 created (one per process: 5 `worn` replacements, none `bloated`). Peak RSS 321 to 357 MiB against the base's 440 to 455, under the 768 MiB threshold. Edit-and-query p50 / p95 / p99 in ms: 433 / 565 / 838 alone, then 498 / 1,115 / 1,700 and 515 / 1,572 / 2,422 against the base's 458 / 605 / 882 and 546 / 1,015 / 1,461 interleaved; over 150 edits, 425 / 1,109 and 422 / 782 against 497 / 825 and 466 / 903. The checker's CPU per edit fell from 437 and 737 ms to 56 and 70; caliper's stayed at 222 to 259. The tails moved with the load more than with the branch, and include the first answer of each new process, which builds afresh. **FAIL** (p95 far above 25 ms).
- **Result, own props.** p50 19.8, p95 22.6, p99 47.7 ms (the p99 is the process replacements), checker CPU 23 ms per edit, peak 229 MiB, every answer equal to a fresh session's. The base: 55.2 / 83.3 / 93.9 ms, checker CPU 350 ms, peak 375 MiB. **PASS** in this form.
- **Byte identity.** The edited component and 10 others (sampled every hundredth key) after 300 edits equal a fresh session's asked in reverse order, 20,282,789 bytes, the same count as the base's, in every run.
- **What bounds the `ButtonProps` form.** Converting the answer, not the checker. The same request on the unchanged snapshot takes 330 to 375 ms (`queryOnlyMs`), almost all of it caliper's: about 4,600 requests and their answers to parse per conversion of Chakra's `ButtonProps` (see [first answer](#fewer-and-cheaper-requests-2026-11-10-perfchecker-first-answer)), which an edit makes again because a type's handle and the memo keyed by it belong to one checker. Meeting 25 ms there needs a conversion that survives the edit: a dependency's types cached by declaration across snapshots, which needs the per-component dependency closure ADR 0026 lists as unsolved.
- **The other gates, re-run.** `just gate-measure` on the branch (exit 1, from first answer and watch): memory PASS (650 of 650 answers the checker's, none stale, 11 processes, 10 `worn` replacements, peak 341 MiB against 446 to 478 before, last answer equal to a fresh session's), determinism PASS (nine outputs of 341,419,093 bytes, all identical, as before), first answer 435 ms over 5 runs (409 to 511; the first answer still builds its snapshot with `createSnapshot`, and its files are stamped after the reply), FAIL as before, and watch 520 / 1,161 / 2,727 ms with the checker's CPU at 80 ms per edit, FAIL on the p95 alone.
- **Verdict and recommendation.** The loud-failure and memory parts PASS. Edit-and-query PASSES at p95 22.6 ms where the edit leaves a small props type in a Chakra-sized program, and FAILS for a component of Chakra's `ButtonProps` (p95 565 ms or more), whose floor is its conversion. Keep 25 ms as the budget for the checker's part (the own-props form, which the harness runs with `--props own`), and give the `ButtonProps` form the first answer's budget and seam: its cost is the same conversion.

The five corpora's budgets are "record on first run".
- **A session's kept answers** (the Storybook addon's configuration through the native binding: lazy, dependencies loaded, nothing collapsed, `semanticWaitMs` and `semanticWaitEmptyMs` 60 s so every answer is the checker's; `gate-large`'s components asked one at a time, the process's RSS read every 100). Watch keeps 25 ms for the checker's own part (own props: p95 6.3 ms in process), and records the `ButtonProps` form: **p95 162.3 ms** (p50 157.7, p99 168.5), whose floor is converting its 1,138 props.

With it, a notified file is read again and the response lists it under `changedFiles`; an unnotified one stays stale, and so does an unnotified file beside a notified one. #!/bin/zsh
# Usage: ab.sh <runs> <extra-args> <binary>... — interleaved extract --json --quiet --no-cache on gate-large and
# Chakra-only; wall, CPU and peak RSS from /usr/bin/time -l, one line per run. extra-args "" for none.
runs=$1; shift
extra=$1; shift
cd /Users/gabe/Projects/caliper-fixtures/perf-analysis
for i in $(seq $runs); do
  for bin in "$@"; do
    for project in gate-large chakra-only; do
      case $project in
        gate-large) src=../gate-large/src ;;
        chakra-only) src=../checker-default/chakra-only/src ;;
      esac
      out=$(/usr/bin/time -l $bin extract --src $src --json --quiet --no-cache ${=extra} 2>&1 >/dev/null)
      real=$(echo "$out" | awk '/real/ {print $1}')
      rss=$(echo "$out" | awk '/maximum resident/ {printf "%d", $1/1048576}')
      cpu=$(echo "$out" | awk '/real/ {print $3+$5}')
      echo "$project $(basename $bin) ${real}s ${rss}MiB cpu=${cpu}s load=$(sysctl -n vm.loadavg | awk '{print $2}')"
    done
  done
done

"""Summarise a samply profile: per thread, top self and inclusive functions. Usage: prof.py <profile.json.gz> [thread-substr] [N] [filter-substr]"""
import gzip
import json
import re
import sys
from collections import Counter

path = sys.argv[1]
want = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None
N = int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 40
needle = sys.argv[4] if len(sys.argv) > 4 else None
p = json.load(gzip.open(path))
syms = json.load(open(path.replace('.json.gz', '.json.syms.json')))
strings = syms['string_table']
libmap = {}
for entry in syms['data']:
    table = sorted(entry['symbol_table'], key=lambda e: e['rva'])
    libmap[entry['code_id']] = table
import bisect
libs = p['libs']
starts = {}
for code, table in libmap.items():
    starts[code] = [e['rva'] for e in table]


def name_of(lib_index, address):
    lib = libs[lib_index]
    code = lib.get('codeId')
    table = libmap.get(code)
    if not table:
        return f'{lib["name"]}+{address:x}'
    i = bisect.bisect_right(starts[code], address) - 1
    if i < 0:
        return f'{lib["name"]}?'
    e = table[i]
    return strings[e['symbol']]


def short(name):
    name = re.sub(r'<[^<>]*>', '', name)
    name = re.sub(r'<[^<>]*>', '', name)
    return name[:150]


for th in p['threads']:
    samples = th['samples']['stack']
    if want and want not in th['name']:
        continue
    if len(samples) < 50:
        continue
    ft, st, ns = th['frameTable'], th['stackTable'], th['nativeSymbols']
    fnames = []
    for i in range(ft['length']):
        func = ft['func'][i]
        res = th['funcTable']['resource'][func]
        lib = th['resourceTable']['lib'][res] if res is not None and res >= 0 else None
        if lib is None:
            fnames.append('?')
        else:
            fnames.append(short(name_of(lib, ft['address'][i])))
    self_c, incl_c = Counter(), Counter()
    total = 0
    for s in samples:
        if s is None:
            continue
        total += 1
        seen = set()
        first = True
        path_names = []
        while s is not None:
            n = fnames[st['frame'][s]]
            path_names.append(n)
            if first:
                self_c[n] += 1
                first = False
            if n not in seen:
                incl_c[n] += 1
                seen.add(n)
            s = st['prefix'][s]
    print(f'=== {th["name"]} samples={total}')
    print('-- self')
    for n, c in self_c.most_common(N):
        if needle and needle not in n:
            continue
        print(f'{c:6d} {100*c/total:5.1f}% {n}')
    print('-- inclusive')
    for n, c in incl_c.most_common(N * 3):
        if needle and needle not in n:
            continue
        print(f'{c:6d} {100*c/total:5.1f}% {n}')

1	//! react-docgen-typescript's `ComponentDoc` shape: the CLI's `--format rdt`, and the `__docgenInfo` Storybook converts
2	//! to argTypes, which the NAPI binding hands the Storybook integration.
3	
4	use crate::types::{ComponentEntry, ExtractionOutput, ParsedProp, PropType};
5	
6	/// RDT's type-name convention for literal unions: `{"name": "enum", "value": [...]}`
7	/// instead of inlining the literal text into `type.name` as a plain string. Lets
8	/// prop-table renderers that pattern-match `type.name === "enum"` (a common
9	/// Storybook addon integration point) show a `<select>` control for the most
10	/// common, most curated props in any design system (variant, size, color…).
11	/// A single string or number literal is a one-option enum, as Storybook's own docgen has it. An enum member's option is
12	/// its value (`"small"` for `Size.Small`, `PropType::option_text`), which is what the control passes.
13	///
14	/// Storybook unquotes each option's source text into a string or a number, so `true` in an enum would reach the control
15	/// as the string "true". A union with a boolean member therefore stays a type name, which Storybook's converter splits
16	/// at the `|` and parses as JSON into the options `["a", 1, true]`, unless a member's text would not survive that (a
17	/// string holding `|`, `"` or `\`); it is then an enum, so that no option is lost.
18	pub fn type_json(prop_type: &PropType) -> serde_json::Value {
19	    if prop_type.is_literal_union() {
20	        let values: Vec<serde_json::Value> = match prop_type {
21	            PropType::Union(members) => members.iter().map(|m| serde_json::json!({"value": m.option_text()})).collect(),
22	            PropType::LiteralUnion { members, .. } => {
23	                members.iter().map(|m| serde_json::json!({"value": format!("\"{m}\"")})).collect()
24	            }
25	            single => vec![serde_json::json!({"value": single.option_text()})],
26	        };
27	        return serde_json::json!({ "name": "enum", "raw": prop_type.raw_string(), "value": values });
28	    }
29	    serde_json::json!({ "name": prop_type.raw_string() })
30	}
31	
32	/// RDT's default `skipChildrenPropWithoutDoc`: an undocumented `children` says nothing a
33	/// prop table can show, so RDT never emits it. Canonical output keeps it.
34	pub fn omits(prop: &ParsedProp) -> bool {
35	    prop.name == "children" && prop.description.is_empty()
36	}
37	
38	/// One component as RDT documents it, except that an undocumented `children` stays: this is the `__docgenInfo`
39	/// Storybook's React renderer converts, and its own docgen lists `children`. `methods` is always `[]` — this tool
40	/// doesn't extract class methods, and Storybook only reads it for class components.
41	pub fn docgen_info(entry: &ComponentEntry) -> serde_json::Value {
42	    component_doc(entry, |_| true)
43	}
44	
45	/// The props a props table lists: the component's own and inherited ones, then the curated attributes inherited from an
46	/// HTML element, which `curated` mode keeps apart so the canonical output can collapse them. A prop named in both is
47	/// listed once, as the component declares it. A prop tagged `@ignore` is left out, as Storybook's own docgen leaves it
48	/// out; the canonical output keeps it.
49	fn component_doc(entry: &ComponentEntry, keep: impl Fn(&ParsedProp) -> bool) -> serde_json::Value {
50	    let props: serde_json::Map<String, serde_json::Value> = entry
51	        .props
52	        .iter()
53	        .chain(entry.notable_inherited.iter().filter(|(name, _)| !entry.props.contains_key(*name)))
54	        .filter(|(_, prop)| keep(prop) && !prop.tags.contains_key("ignore"))
55	        .map(|(k, prop)| {
56	            let obj = serde_json::json!({
57	                "name": prop.name,
58	                "type": type_json(&prop.prop_type),
59	                "required": prop.required,
60	                "defaultValue": prop.default_value.as_ref().map(|d| serde_json::json!({"value": d.value, "computed": d.computed})),
61	                "description": prop.description,
62	                "parent": prop.parent.as_ref().map(|p| serde_json::json!({"name": p.name, "fileName": p.file_name})),
63	            });
64	            (k.clone(), obj)
65	        })
66	        .collect();
67	    serde_json::json!({
68	        "displayName": entry.display_name,
69	        "props": serde_json::Value::Object(props),
70	        "description": entry.description,
71	        "methods": [],
72	        "tags": entry.tags,
73	        "composes": entry.composes,
74	    })
75	}
76	
77	/// The components of `output` as RDT documents them, keyed as in the output, pretty-printed. Like RDT, only exported
78	/// components unless `include_unexported`, each with RDT's `filePath`, which `__docgenInfo` doesn't carry.
79	pub fn serialize(output: &ExtractionOutput, include_unexported: bool) -> serde_json::Result<String> {
80	    let map: serde_json::Map<String, serde_json::Value> = output
81	        .components
82	        .iter()
83	        .filter(|(_, entry)| include_unexported || entry.exported)
84	        .map(|(name, entry)| {
85	            let mut doc = component_doc(entry, |prop| !omits(prop));
86	            doc["filePath"] = serde_json::json!(entry.file_path);
87	            (name.clone(), doc)
88	        })
89	        .collect();
90	    serde_json::to_string_pretty(&serde_json::Value::Object(map))
91	}
